etymology: From binnacle, the stand or housing that holds the ship’s compass, and list. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) says the list of men unable to report for duty was given to the officer of the watch and kept at the binnacle, or placed on it each morning so the captain knew the health of his crew. NHHC dates the practice to the eighteenth century and probably earlier.
biblical_def: The binnacle list is the Navy’s sick list: the names of the men excused from duty because of illness or injury. The binnacle is the stand on which the compass is mounted, and NHHC records that the list was kept there, where the officer of the watch would see it. NHHC also notes that new sailors often confused binnacle with barnacle and wondered what their sickness had to do with the growths on the hull. The Christian observation: a ship keeps a written account of its sick because a captain must know the true strength of his crew, and the weak must not be overlooked. Christ said, “They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick” (Mat 9:12). The church is told the same thing in practical terms: “Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church” (Jas 5:14). The sick are to be named, prayed over and cared for, and “The LORD will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing” (Psa 41:3).
webster_summary: The Navy’s sick list, named for the binnacle (the compass stand) where it was kept for the officer of the watch (NHHC). The sick are to be named and cared for, not hidden (Jas 5:14).
webster_full: BINNACLE LIST, n. (Navy) The list of crew members excused from duty because of sickness or injury. From binnacle, the housing of the ship’s compass, where the list was kept (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Mat 9:12
But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
Jas 5:14
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
Psa 41:3
The LORD will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness.
corruption_summary: A sick list exists so the weak are cared for; it is abused when a man hides on it from his duty, or hides from it out of pride.
corruption_paragraphs: Any list of the excused can be abused in two directions. One man shelters on it to escape work he could do. Another refuses to be put on it at all, because he will not admit weakness, and the whole crew pays for his pride.

Scripture rebukes both. The idle are told to work with their own hands (1Th 4:11), and the proud are told to confess their need and call for help (Jas 5:14). A church that keeps no account of its sick has stopped watching over its people.
roots_summary: binnacle (compass stand) + list → binnacle list, the sick list kept where the officer of the watch would see it (NHHC: eighteenth century and probably before).
roots_lines: binnacle: the stand or housing that holds the ship’s compass
Eighteenth century and probably before: the list of men unfit for duty kept at the binnacle (NHHC)
Modern Navy: binnacle list still means the sick list
usage: “Three men from the deck division were on the binnacle list with the flu.”
They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. (Mat 9:12).

pos: noun (Navy); in the phrase to the bitter end
etymology: Nautical. A bitt is a wooden or iron post set through a ship’s deck to make lines fast. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that a turn of line around a bitt is called a bitter, so the last part of the line, secured to the bitts, is the bitter end. Sailors now use it for the end of any line, and landsmen took it up in “to the bitter end.”
biblical_def: The bitter end is the inboard end of a line or anchor cable, the part made fast to the bitts on deck. When the cable has run out to the bitter end, there is nothing more to pay out. NHHC records that ashore the phrase became “stick to the bitter end” and “faithful to the bitter end,” used of anyone who keeps to a course whatever it costs. The word has nothing to do with bitterness; it comes from the bitts. The Christian observation: the Christian life is a line paid out to its last fathom. “He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13). We are partakers of Christ “if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end” (Heb 3:14). And the Lord’s word to the church at Smyrna is the bitter end made glorious: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).
webster_summary: The inboard end of a line or cable, made fast to the bitts (NHHC); hence to the bitter end, to the very last. Faithfulness unto death (Rev 2:10).
webster_full: BITTER END, n. (Navy) The end of a line or cable secured to the bitts; in general use, the end of any line. From bitt, a deck post, and bitter, a turn of line around it (Naval History and Heritage Command).
TO THE BITTER END, phr. To the very last, whatever the consequences.
scriptures: But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
Heb 3:14
For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end;
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
corruption_summary: NHHC notes the shore phrase can describe holding a course “without regard to consequences”; stubbornness in a wrong course is not the perseverance Scripture praises.
corruption_paragraphs: “To the bitter end” can praise two very different men. One holds to the truth when it costs him everything. The other holds to his own plan because he will not admit he was wrong. The phrase sounds the same for both, and pride is glad of the cover.

Scripture’s perseverance is faithfulness to Christ, not loyalty to one’s own course. The saints endure because God keeps them, and they hold fast to the confidence they began with (Heb 3:14). A man who has run out his line in the wrong direction is called to repent, not to admire his own grit.
roots_summary: bitt (deck post) → bitter (a turn of line around it) → bitter end, the last of the line at the bitts → to the bitter end ashore (NHHC).
roots_lines: bitt: a wooden or iron post through a ship’s deck for securing lines
bitter: a turn of line around a bitt
Ashore: “stick to the bitter end,” “faithful to the bitter end” (NHHC)
usage: “Veer the cable, but not to the bitter end.”
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. (Mat 24:13).

etymology: Sailors’ name for the galley smokestack. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) says it is said to come from a British merchant captain, Charles Noble, who about 1850 found that his galley stack was copper and ordered it kept polished, so the crew called it the “Charley Noble.” NHHC gives this as a reported origin, not a documented one.
biblical_def: Charley Noble is the galley stack or funnel, the chimney that carries the cooking smoke out of the ship. NHHC stresses that Charley Noble “is an ‘it,’ not a ‘he,’” and records the custom of sending green recruits off to find Charley Noble, a hunt that amuses the veterans. The story behind the name is a captain who insisted that a copper smokestack be kept bright, a small, hot, dirty job that no inspector would usually notice. The Christian observation: the faithful man does the small duty well because God sees it, not because the captain is watching. “Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). Paul told servants to obey “not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God” (Col 3:22). And our Lord gave the rule: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10).
webster_summary: Sailors’ name for the galley smokestack; said to come from a merchant captain, Charles Noble, who about 1850 had his copper stack kept bright (NHHC). Faithful in the least (Luk 16:10).
webster_full: CHARLEY NOBLE (also Charlie Noble), n. (Navy) The galley smokestack or funnel. Said to be named for Charles Noble, a British merchant captain about 1850 (Naval History and Heritage Command; reported origin).
Custom note: green recruits are sent to look for Charley Noble, to the amusement of the crew (NHHC).
scriptures: Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Col 3:22
Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God:
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
corruption_summary: Eyeservice polishes only what the inspector will look at; the Christian keeps the unseen stack bright because the Lord sees it.
corruption_paragraphs: Every crew learns where the inspector looks, and the temptation is to make those places shine and let the rest go. Scripture calls that eyeservice and sets it against singleness of heart (Col 3:22). Work done only to be seen is a kind of lie about the ship.
The galley stack is a fair test. It is hot, sooty and out of the way. A man who keeps it bright when no one asks has learned the lesson of Luk 16:10, and he is the man who can be trusted with much.
roots_summary: Capt. Charles Noble (reported, about 1850) → copper galley stack kept polished → Charley Noble, the galley smokestack (NHHC).
roots_lines: About 1850: a British merchant captain, Charles Noble, is said to have ordered his copper galley stack kept bright (NHHC)
Navy custom: recruits sent to find Charley Noble (NHHC)
usage: “The boot spent half the watch looking for Charley Noble.”
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. (Col 3:23).

etymology: Origin uncertain. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) records two explanations: that dog is a corruption of dodge, because the short watches let men dodge standing the same watch every day, or that it refers to the fitful sleep called “dog sleep.” NHHC concludes that “no one really knows the origin of this term,” which was in use at least back to 1700.
biblical_def: A dogwatch is one of the two short watches at sea: the first dogwatch from 4 to 6 p.m. and the second from 6 to 8 p.m. The other watches run four hours each: afternoon, first night watch, mid watch, morning watch and forenoon watch. NHHC explains that the evening period was split in two so that the same sailors are not on duty at the same hours every day. The name is old, at least as old as 1700, and its source is uncertain. The Christian observation: the watch rotates, but the duty of watching never stops. Our Lord told His disciples, “Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning” (Mar 13:35), which reads like a list of the watches. Men must be relieved; God is never relieved: “he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Psa 121:4). And without Him, “the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1).
webster_summary: Either of the two short evening watches at sea (1600–1800 and 1800–2000), split so the same men do not always stand the same hours; origin unknown, in use by 1700 (NHHC). God neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psa 121:4).
webster_full: DOGWATCH (also dog watch), n. (Navy) The first dogwatch, 1600–1800, or the second dogwatch, 1800–2000. The split rotates the watch bill so that the same sailors are not always on duty at the same time of day.
Origin note: explained as from dodge watch or from dog sleep; NHHC says no one really knows.
scriptures: Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning:
Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.
Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
corruption_summary: A watch kept as routine is not a watch; the danger is the sailor who stands his hours and sees nothing, and the Christian who trusts his own vigilance instead of the Keeper of Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: The rotation of the watch is wise; it spreads the load and keeps men fresh. But a man can stand every hour on the bill and keep no watch at all, because his mind is below decks. Christ’s warning is to the watchman who is present and asleep (Mar 13:36–37).
The opposite error is the man who thinks the ship is safe because he is awake. “Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1). Watching is a duty; safety is a gift.
roots_summary: Short watches 1600–1800 and 1800–2000 → dogwatch (by 1700); explained as dodge watch or dog sleep, origin unknown (NHHC).
roots_lines: Watch bill: afternoon, first and second dogwatch, first night, mid, morning, forenoon (NHHC)
In use at least back to 1700 (NHHC)
Proposed sources: dodge watch; dog sleep. Neither proven
usage: “We ate early and took the second dogwatch.”
Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. (Psa 121:4).

etymology: Navy slang for falsifying reports or records. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) calls the origin “somewhat obscure” and gives two explanations: the false gundeck of British sailing warships, a deck that carried no guns and so misrepresented the ship’s armament; or midshipmen who went below to the gundeck and worked their navigation problems backwards from a dead-reckoning position instead of from real sights. NHHC thinks the second more plausible.
biblical_def: To gundeck a report is to fill it in without doing the work it records: a log entry, an inspection sheet or a maintenance record completed from guesswork and dressed up to look real. NHHC traces two possible sources. One is the deck below the upper deck on British ships of war, called the gundeck though it carried no guns, perhaps to mislead an enemy about the ship’s strength. The other, which NHHC prefers, is the midshipman who was supposed to take sun lines at noon and star sights at night and work them out below on the gundeck, but instead copied the dead-reckoning position and worked backwards to the right answer. Either way the word means a false record. The Christian observation: at sea a falsified record is not a small sin, because men steer by it. “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Pro 11:1). “Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight” (Pro 12:22). Paul gives the reason: “putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another” (Eph 4:25).
webster_summary: Navy slang for falsifying a report or record; traced by NHHC to a false gundeck or to midshipmen faking their navigation work. A false balance is abomination to the LORD (Pro 11:1).
webster_full: GUNDECK, v.t. (Navy slang) To falsify a report, log or record, especially by filling it in without doing the work. GUNDECKING, n. The practice.
Origin note: NHHC calls the origin obscure and offers the false gundeck of British warships and midshipmen’s faked navigation as explanations.
scriptures: Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
Eph 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
corruption_summary: Gundecking treats a record as a form to satisfy rather than a truth to tell; the lie looks harmless on paper and runs ships aground.
corruption_paragraphs: The gundecked report is usually excused as paperwork nobody reads. But a log, a gauge reading or a maintenance card is written so that someone else can act on it. The man who invents it has put his guess in place of the facts and signed his name to it.

The midshipman who works backwards to the expected answer has learned to please the navigator, not to find the ship. Scripture gives no room for that: the just weight is God’s delight (Pro 11:1), and we tell the truth because we are members one of another (Eph 4:25).
roots_summary: gundeck (deck below the upper deck) → false gundeck, or midshipmen’s faked sights worked below → gundeck, to falsify a record (NHHC: origin obscure).
roots_lines: Explanation 1: the British gundeck that carried no guns, a deception about armament (NHHC)
Explanation 2, preferred by NHHC: midshipmen working navigation backwards from dead reckoning on the gundeck
Modern Navy: falsifying reports and records
usage: “Do the readings; don’t gundeck the log.”
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight. (Pro 12:22).

etymology: A soft sandstone used to scrub a ship’s decks. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) gives two explanations for the name: sailors had to kneel to use it, as if in prayer, and it was full of holes. The source does not decide between them.
biblical_def: A holystone is a soft sandstone that sailors used to scrub the decks of a ship; to holystone is to scrub a deck that way. NHHC records that the men had to kneel to do it, “as if in prayer,” and that the stone was full of holes, and either may account for the name. It was hard, wet, knee-wearing work, done so that the decks would be clean. The Christian observation: the picture of a man on his knees scrubbing a deck white is close to the Psalmist’s prayer, “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psa 51:7). But the true cleansing of the church is not done by our scrubbing. Christ gave Himself for her “That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word” (Eph 5:26), “That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle” (Eph 5:27).
webster_summary: A soft sandstone for scrubbing decks; named, NHHC says, either because men knelt to use it as if in prayer or because it is full of holes. Christ cleanses His church by the word (Eph 5:26).
webster_full: HOLYSTONE, n. (Navy) A soft sandstone used to scrub a ship’s decks. v.t. To scrub a deck with it.
Origin note: NHHC gives two explanations, the kneeling posture and the stone’s holes.
scriptures: Psa 51:7
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Eph 5:26
That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word,
Eph 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
corruption_summary: Scrubbing makes a clean deck, not a clean heart; the error is to think that kneeling labour, by itself, washes away sin.
corruption_paragraphs: A sailor on his knees with a holystone is doing honest work, and the deck is the better for it. The error comes when outward scrubbing is taken for inward cleansing. Every religion of works is a holystone religion: kneel long enough and the stain will come out.

David knew better. He asked God to purge him (Psa 51:7), because no labour of his could. The church is made clean by Christ’s giving of Himself and the washing of the word (Eph 5:26). Our scrubbing follows that cleansing; it never replaces it.
roots_summary: Soft sandstone → holystone, for scrubbing decks on one’s knees → to holystone (NHHC: from the kneeling posture or from the holes).
roots_lines: Soft sandstone used to scrub the decks (NHHC)
Name explained by the kneeling, as if in prayer, or by the holes in the stone (NHHC)
usage: “The watch holystoned the quarterdeck before colors.”
Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. (Psa 51:7).

etymology: A borrowing from Dutch kielhalen, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1666, in the London Gazette. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) says the punishment was said to have originated with the Dutch and was adopted by other navies in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
biblical_def: To keelhaul was to drag a man under the hull of a ship as a punishment. NHHC describes it from a 1634 source, Nathaniel Boteler’s A Dialogicall Discourse: a rope was rigged from yardarm to yardarm under the ship, the offender was tied to it, sometimes with weights on his legs, dropped into the sea, hauled under the keel and hoisted up the other side, and the punishment was repeated once he had his breath again. The barnacles on the hull could tear him badly, and NHHC’s second account says few survived. NHHC states that the U.S. Navy never practiced keelhauling, and that all navies abandoned it long ago. Today to keelhaul a man is only to give him a severe dressing-down. The Christian observation: God’s law set a limit even on lawful punishment. “Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed… then thy brother should seem vile unto thee” (Deu 25:3). “The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel” (Pro 12:10). The Lord’s own chastening is grievous for a time, but “afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Heb 12:11); it aims to restore, not to destroy.
webster_summary: To drag an offender under a ship’s keel as punishment (from Dutch kielhalen; OED earliest 1666); now, to rebuke severely. The U.S. Navy never practiced it (NHHC). God’s law limits punishment (Deu 25:3).
webster_full: KEELHAUL, v.t. (from 1666, OED) 1. To haul an offender under the keel of a ship from one side to the other, as a punishment. 2. In modern use, to rebuke severely. From Dutch kielhalen.
History note: said to have originated with the Dutch and adopted by other navies in the 15th–16th centuries; never practiced by the U.S. Navy (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Deu 25:3
Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.
A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
corruption_summary: Keelhauling was discipline turned into cruelty; Scripture’s chastening has a limit and a goal, and punishment without either is not justice.
corruption_paragraphs: Order at sea is a real need, and Scripture does not forbid punishment. But keelhauling had no measure in it. It was built to terrify, it often killed, and it treated a man as something to be destroyed for the crew to see. Moses forbade exactly this: a punishment so heavy that “thy brother should seem vile unto thee” (Deu 25:3).

The opposite error is softer and common now: to treat all correction as cruelty. Scripture rejects both. The Lord chastens those He loves, and the chastening is grievous, but it is measured and it aims at the peaceable fruit of righteousness (Heb 12:11).
roots_summary: Dutch kielhalen → English keelhaul (OED earliest 1666) → naval punishment, said to be Dutch, 15th–16th c. (NHHC) → modern sense, a severe rebuke.
roots_lines: Dutch kielhalen: to haul under the keel (OED etymon)
1634: described in Nathaniel Boteler’s A Dialogicall Discourse (quoted by NHHC)
1666: OED’s earliest evidence, London Gazette
usage: “The chief keelhauled him for leaving the hatch open.”
The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel. (Pro 12:10).

etymology: Formed within English as a compound of midship and man, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1652, in Severall Proceedings in Parliament. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that the boys training as officers on British ships carried orders from the officers aft to the crew forward, through the middle of the ship.
biblical_def: A midshipman was a boy or young man aboard a British warship in training to become a naval officer. NHHC says his chief duty was carrying orders from the officers, quartered in the stern, to the crew in the forecastle, and that this constant running through the middle of the ship gave him his name and the nickname “middie.” In the days of sail a midshipman could begin his career as young as eight. Students at the U.S. Naval Academy and NROTC candidates are still called midshipmen, because they too are officers in training. The Christian observation: the Navy has always trusted the young with real duty under authority, and Scripture does the same. Paul told Timothy, “Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers” (1Ti 4:12). “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth” (Lam 3:27). And the training of the young is commanded: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6).
webster_summary: An officer in training: once a boy on a British warship who carried orders through the middle of the ship (NHHC); now a Naval Academy or NROTC student. From midship + man (OED earliest 1652). Bear the yoke in youth (Lam 3:27).
webster_full: MIDSHIPMAN, n. (from 1652, OED) 1. Formerly, a boy or young man on a warship in training for a commission. 2. A student at the U.S. Naval Academy or in NROTC. From midship + man.
History note: named for carrying orders from the officers aft to the crew forward through the middle of the ship; could begin at age eight (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Lam 3:27
It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: The old navy put boys under real duty and authority; an age that keeps young men from responsibility until late, then wonders why they do not lead, has forgotten the midshipman.
corruption_paragraphs: A midshipman learned command by carrying orders before he gave them. He was young, he was under authority, and the work was real. Modern culture tends to stretch boyhood out and shelter the young from consequence, then expects leadership to appear in a man of thirty.

Scripture expects youth to be a time of training under the yoke (Lam 3:27) and of example, not exemption (1Ti 4:12). Fathers and churches that hand young men real duty, and stand over them while they learn it, are doing what the old navy did.
roots_summary: midship + man (OED earliest 1652) → boy carrying orders through the middle of the ship (NHHC) → officer in training → Naval Academy midshipman.
roots_lines: 1652: OED’s earliest evidence, Severall Proceedings in Parliament
Days of sail: duties included carrying orders from aft to forward; careers could begin at eight (NHHC)
Today: U.S. Naval Academy students and NROTC candidates
usage: “He reported to Annapolis as a midshipman.”
It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth. (Lam 3:27).

pos: noun (Navy); in the smoking lamp is lighted / is out
etymology: A compound of smoking and lamp. The Oxford English Dictionary records its earliest evidence in 1889, in the Century Dictionary. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) says the exact date and origin of the lamp itself “has been lost,” but that it probably came into use in the sixteenth century, when seamen began smoking aboard ship.
biblical_def: The smoking lamp was an oil lamp hung in one place aboard a wooden ship, from which the men lit their pipes and cigars. NHHC explains it as a safety measure: fire was the great enemy of a ship built of timber and carrying gunpowder, so smoking was allowed only at certain times and in one area, usually the forecastle or near the galley, where the lamp hung. “The smoking lamp is lighted” meant smoking was permitted; “the smoking lamp is out” meant it was not. The lamps are gone, but the order survives as a figure of speech, given before drills, refueling and taking on ammunition. The Christian observation: one small, controlled flame kept a whole ship from burning. Solomon asked, “Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?” (Pro 6:27). James applies it to speech: “Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!” (Jas 3:5). And the rule that kept the lamp in its place is Paul’s: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: The single lamp aboard ship from which men lit tobacco, at set times and places, to keep fire from timber and powder (NHHC; OED earliest 1889); now an order permitting or forbidding smoking. A little fire kindles a great matter (Jas 3:5).
webster_full: SMOKING LAMP, n. (from 1889, OED) (Navy) The lamp from which sailors were allowed to light pipes and cigars at authorized times and places. The smoking lamp is lighted: smoking is permitted. The smoking lamp is out: smoking is forbidden.
History note: origin of the lamp lost; probably 16th century; a fire-safety measure (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Pro 6:27
Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?
Jas 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: The smoking lamp kept a small fire in its place; the danger has always been the man who thinks his own small fire is harmless.
corruption_paragraphs: No sailor meant to burn his ship. Ships burned because one man thought his pipe, his candle or his spark was too small to matter. The smoking lamp answered that with a rule: one flame, one place, set times.

Sin and the tongue work the same way (Jas 3:5). The man who carries fire in his bosom always believes he can manage it (Pro 6:27). Wisdom keeps the small fires under order, because order is what keeps the ship afloat (1Co 14:40).
roots_summary: Oil lamp for lighting tobacco, probably 16th century (NHHC) → smoking lamp (OED earliest 1889) → “the smoking lamp is lighted / is out” as an order.
roots_lines: 16th century (probably): seamen begin smoking aboard; the lamp follows (NHHC)
1889: OED’s earliest evidence, Century Dictionary
Today: the order survives before drills, refueling and ammunition handling (NHHC)
usage: “The smoking lamp is out while taking on fuel.”
Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth! (Jas 3:5).

etymology: The Oxford English Dictionary analyses it as a compound formed within English from ward (n.2) and room, with its earliest evidence in 1759, in the Annual Register 1758, under the subject “navy.” The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) tells a different story: that it was once the wardrobe, a compartment on eighteenth-century British ships for storing booty, where the officers took to eating when it was empty. The two accounts do not agree.
biblical_def: The wardroom is the officers’ mess and lounge aboard a warship. NHHC’s account is that the room began as a wardrobe for storing prizes taken at sea, near the officers’ mess and staterooms, and that when it stood empty the officers gathered there to eat; when the days of pirating ended it became their mess for good and was raised in name from a wardrobe to a wardroom. The OED does not support the wardrobe story and treats the word as ward + room. NHHC also records that chaplains were not admitted to the wardroom until the eighteenth century. The Christian observation: a common table makes a body out of a group of men. “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith” (Pro 15:17). “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psa 133:1). And the rule of that table is “in honour preferring one another” (Rom 12:10).
webster_summary: The officers’ mess aboard a warship (OED earliest 1759, as ward + room; NHHC derives it from a booty “wardrobe”). Brethren in unity (Psa 133:1).
webster_full: WARDROOM, n. (from 1759, OED) The mess and lounge of the officers on a warship. Compound of ward and room (OED).
Origin note: NHHC derives it from the “wardrobe” where booty was stored on 18th-century British ships; the OED analysis differs.
scriptures: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
corruption_summary: A wardroom is meant to bind officers into one body; when rank and rivalry rule the table, the dinner is a stalled ox with hatred.
corruption_paragraphs: Every mess can turn into a court where men jockey for place. A ship whose officers eat together but do not trust one another has a wardroom in name only, and the crew will feel it. Solomon’s proverb is a fair verdict: plain food with love beats a feast with hatred (Pro 15:17).

Paul’s rule for the household of God fits the wardroom too: brotherly love, and in honour preferring one another (Rom 12:10). The officer who seeks the lower seat makes the table what it was meant to be.
roots_summary: ward + room (OED; earliest 1759) → officers’ mess. NHHC’s alternative: booty wardrobe → wardroom.
roots_lines: 1759: OED’s earliest evidence, Annual Register 1758; OED subjects navy (mid 1700s), military (1850s)
NHHC account: 18th-century British “wardrobe” for prizes, used by the officers as a mess
Chaplains admitted to the wardroom only from the 18th century (NHHC)
usage: “The captain dined with the wardroom on Sunday.”
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! (Psa 133:1).

etymology: A compound of sick and bay. The Oxford English Dictionary records its earliest evidence in 1813, in the writing of John Thomson, physician and surgeon. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that sick berths on sailing ships were in the rounded stern, whose shape suggested a bay.
biblical_def: The sick bay is the place aboard ship, or at a naval station, where sailors receive medical care. NHHC notes that in the days of sail there were few places ashore set aside for ill seamen, but most ships had sick berths in the rounded stern, and the curve of the stern suggested the shape of a bay, so the sailors called them sickbays. The Christian observation: a ship carries its own place of mercy, because at sea there is no other. Christ counts the care of the sick as care of Himself: “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36). The Samaritan “bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine… and took care of him” (Luk 10:34). And behind every human healer stands the Lord who “healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psa 147:3).
webster_summary: The medical space aboard ship or at a naval station (OED earliest 1813); NHHC explains the name from sick berths in a ship’s rounded stern. “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36).
webster_full: SICK BAY (also sickbay), n. (from 1813, OED) The compartment of a ship, or the building at a naval station, where the sick and injured are treated.
Origin note: sick berths in the rounded stern, shaped like a bay (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
corruption_summary: The sick bay is mercy built into the ship; the danger is to leave all care of the sick to professionals and forget that Christ calls every disciple to visit them.
corruption_paragraphs: A ship’s doctor and corpsmen are a gift, and the church rightly honours medicine. But it is easy for a congregation to assume that because the sick are in skilled hands they need nothing from the rest of us.

Christ’s words in Mat 25:36 are addressed to ordinary disciples, not to physicians. The visit, the prayer and the meal are still the church’s work, and the Lord who binds up wounds (Psa 147:3) uses His people to do it.
roots_summary: sick + bay → sick berths in the rounded stern of sailing ships (NHHC) → sick bay (OED earliest 1813).
roots_lines: Days of sail: sick berths in the rounded stern, shaped like a bay (NHHC)
1813: OED’s earliest evidence, John Thomson, physician and surgeon
usage: “Report to sick bay and have that hand looked at.”
I was sick, and ye visited me. (Mat 25:36).

etymology: From the proper name Jacob and ladder, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1733, in a dictionary by the horticulturist Philip Miller, and lists the nautical sense from the 1840s. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) says the name alludes to the patriarch Jacob, who dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven (Gen 28:12).
biblical_def: A Jacob’s ladder is a portable ladder of rope or metal, used primarily as an aid in boarding ship. NHHC says the name first belonged to a network of line leading up to the skysail on wooden ships, and that it alludes to the biblical Jacob, adding that anyone who has climbed one with a seabag can see why: the climb seems long enough to reach the next world. The OED also records the name as a plant name from 1733. The source is Genesis: Jacob, fleeing from Esau, slept at Bethel and “dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Gen 28:12). He woke and said, “this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Gen 28:17). Christ identified Himself as that ladder: “Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man” (Joh 1:51).
webster_summary: A portable rope or metal ladder for boarding ship; named for Jacob’s dream at Bethel (Gen 28:12; OED; NHHC). Christ is the true ladder between heaven and earth (Joh 1:51).
webster_full: JACOB’S LADDER, n. (from 1733, OED; nautical from the 1840s) 1. (Nautical) A portable ladder of rope or metal used for boarding a ship; originally rigging leading to the skysail. 2. A plant name. From Jacob and ladder, after Gen 28:12.
Origin note: the allusion to Jacob’s dream is given by the Naval History and Heritage Command.
scriptures: And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
Joh 1:51
And he saith unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
corruption_summary: The ship’s ladder is climbed by a man’s own strength; Jacob’s ladder was set down by God, and the error is to make it a picture of climbing to heaven by effort.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase is often used as a picture of spiritual ascent: rung by rung, the soul works its way up to God. That reading has a long history in mystical writing, and it turns the text upside down. Jacob did not climb anything. He was a fugitive asleep on a stone, and God set the ladder up and spoke to him from above it.
Christ settles the meaning in Joh 1:51. He is the ladder, the one Mediator between God and men. The traffic on it is angels and grace coming down to sinners, not sinners climbing up by merit.
roots_summary: Jacob’s dream at Bethel (Gen 28:12) → Jacob’s ladder (OED earliest 1733, a plant name) → nautical rigging and boarding ladder (OED 1840s; NHHC).
roots_lines: Gen 28:12: the ladder of Jacob’s dream
1733: OED’s earliest evidence, Philip Miller’s dictionary (plant sense)
1840s: nautical sense (OED); originally line leading to the skysail (NHHC)
usage: “The pilot came up the Jacob’s ladder in a heavy swell.”
This is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven. (Gen 28:17).

etymology: A compound of port (n.3, an opening or gate) and hole, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1569, in a translation by Thomas Stocker, with early senses in gunnery and the navy. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that the name has nothing to do with the port side: it comes from the French porte, a door, used for the gun ports cut in a ship’s side.
biblical_def: A porthole is an opening in the side of a ship. NHHC answers the novice’s question of why holes on the starboard side are not called starboard-holes: the word has nothing to do with location. It began with the gun ports cut through a ship’s sides so that heavy cannon could be mounted inside the hull, with covers for heavy weather; porte, French for door, gave the name, and in time it came to mean any opening in a ship’s side. The OED’s earliest evidence is from 1569, under gunnery and navy. The Christian observation: the first ship in Scripture was built with an opening by God’s own specification: “A window shalt thou make to the ark” (Gen 6:16). At the end of the flood, “Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made” (Gen 8:6) and sent out the birds to find land. And the LORD uses the same picture for His provision: “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing” (Mal 3:10).
webster_summary: An opening in a ship’s side, first for guns, later any opening; from port, door (French porte), + hole (OED earliest 1569; NHHC). A window shalt thou make to the ark (Gen 6:16).
webster_full: PORTHOLE, n. (from 1569, OED) 1. Originally, an opening in a ship’s side through which a gun was fired. 2. Any opening in a ship’s side, for cannon or not. From port (an opening) + hole.
Origin note: not from the port side; from French porte, door (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Gen 6:16
A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it.
Gen 8:6
And it came to pass at the end of forty days, that Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made:
Mal 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
corruption_summary: The porthole began as a gun port and became a window; the error is to assume a word means what it seems to say, as the novice does with port and starboard.
corruption_paragraphs: Every sailor who guessed that portholes belong on the port side made the most common mistake in word study: reading the meaning off the surface. The word’s history corrected him. Many errors about Scripture start the same way, with an English word taken at face value instead of in its own setting.

The cure is the one the Bereans used: search it out (Act 17:11). A word’s meaning is what its users meant by it, and the meaning of a text is what God said in it, not what it seems to say to a hurried reader.
roots_summary: port (opening, door; French porte) + hole → gun port (OED earliest 1569, gunnery and navy) → any opening in a ship’s side.
roots_lines: 1569: OED’s earliest evidence, Thomas Stocker’s translation; OED subjects gunnery and navy (mid 1500s)
Gun ports cut in the side for heavy cannon, with covers for heavy weather (NHHC)
Later: any opening in a ship’s side, for cannon or not (NHHC)
usage: “Dog down that porthole before the weather hits.”
A window shalt thou make to the ark. (Gen 6:16).

etymology: The Oxford English Dictionary treats the verb skylark as formed within English by conversion from the noun skylark, the bird, with its earliest evidence in 1771, in the Proceedings of the Old Bailey. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) gives a different account: that young sailors’ play high in the masts was first “skylacing,” from an old word lac, to play, later corrupted to skylarking. The two accounts do not agree.
biblical_def: Skylarking is horseplay and fooling around on duty. NHHC says it first described the antics of young sailors who climbed the rigging and slid down the backstays for fun. In the days of wooden ships it was thought better for idle men to skylark on the weather deck than to talk mutiny in a dark corner of the ship. Today it is frowned on aboard ship, because goofing off causes accidents and wastes time. The OED connects the verb with the bird, the skylark that climbs high and sings, not with NHHC’s lac. The Christian observation: Scripture makes room for play, but not for foolery that does harm. There is “a time to laugh” and “a time to dance” (Ecc 3:4). But “It is as sport to a fool to do mischief” (Pro 10:23), and the Christian is told, “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time” (Eph 5:15–16).
webster_summary: Horseplay or fooling around, first of young sailors playing in the rigging (NHHC); OED derives the verb from the bird, earliest 1771. A time to laugh (Ecc 3:4), but walk circumspectly (Eph 5:15).
webster_full: SKYLARK, v.i. (from 1771, OED) To frolic or play about; originally of sailors in the rigging. SKYLARKING, n. Horseplay, especially on duty.
Origin note: OED, from the bird skylark; NHHC, from “skylacing,” with lac, to play.
scriptures: Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
It is as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom.
Eph 5:15
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
corruption_summary: Play has its time; skylarking is play out of its time and place, where a man’s fun becomes another man’s danger.
corruption_paragraphs: The old navy saw that idle young men will do something with their energy, and preferred the rigging to mutiny. That is a real insight: men need an outlet. But the outlet became a hazard once the play moved into working spaces and working hours.

Scripture neither forbids laughter nor makes it a law of its own. The question is time and place (Ecc 3:4). Mischief done for sport is the fool’s pleasure (Pro 10:23); the wise man redeems the time (Eph 5:16).
roots_summary: skylark (the bird) → skylark v., to frolic (OED earliest 1771) → skylarking, sailors’ horseplay (NHHC; NHHC’s alternative: skylacing).
roots_lines: 1771: OED’s earliest evidence for the verb, Proceedings Old Bailey; the noun skylark from the late 1600s
Days of sail: young sailors climbing and sliding down the backstays (NHHC)
Today: discouraged aboard ship as a cause of accidents (NHHC)
usage: “Knock off the skylarking and secure that line.”
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise. (Eph 5:15).

etymology: The Oxford English Dictionary gives it as a compound of English pea and coat, with its earliest evidence in 1790, in the Pennsylvania Packet. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains pea from “pilot cloth,” sometimes called P-cloth, which made a “p-jacket” and later a pea coat; NHHC dates the term to 1723, earlier than the OED’s first evidence. The two accounts differ.
biblical_def: A pea coat is the heavy topcoat worn by seafaring men in cold, miserable weather. NHHC says the name does not come from pea-soup weather. The coat was once tailored from pilot cloth, a heavy, coarse, stout twilled blue cloth with the nap on one side; the cloth was sometimes called P-cloth from its initial letter, the garment a p-jacket, and later a pea coat. The OED’s earliest record is 1790. The Christian observation: warm clothing against the cold is a mark of good provision in Scripture. The virtuous woman “is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet” (Pro 31:21). Paul, in prison and near the end, asked Timothy to bring “The cloke that I left at Troas” (2Ti 4:13). And Job counted it righteousness that he had not “seen any perish for want of clothing” (Job 31:19).
webster_summary: A sailor’s heavy cold-weather topcoat (OED earliest 1790); NHHC derives it from pilot cloth or P-cloth. A household clothed against the snow (Pro 31:21).
webster_full: PEA COAT (also peacoat), n. (from 1790, OED) A heavy topcoat worn by sailors in cold weather. Compound of pea and coat (OED).
Origin note: NHHC derives pea from pilot cloth, called P-cloth, and dates the term to 1723.
scriptures: She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet.
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering;
corruption_summary: A pea coat is plain provision against the weather; the error is to treat clothing as display instead of covering, and to forget the poor who have none.
corruption_paragraphs: The pea coat has been adopted ashore as fashion, and there is no harm in a good coat. But Scripture’s interest in clothing is covering and provision. The household clothed in scarlet is warm (Pro 31:21), and Paul wanted his cloak because the prison was cold (2Ti 4:13).
Job’s test is the one that matters: did anyone perish for want of clothing while he had it to give (Job 31:19)? A Christian’s wardrobe is measured by what it covers, including what it gives away.
roots_summary: pea + coat (OED earliest 1790). NHHC: pilot cloth → P-cloth → p-jacket → pea coat (NHHC date 1723).
roots_lines: Pilot cloth: heavy, coarse, twilled blue cloth with the nap on one side (NHHC)
1790: OED’s earliest evidence, Pennsylvania Packet
usage: “It was cold on the pier, and every man had his pea coat buttoned to the collar.”
She is not afraid of the snow for her household. (Pro 31:21).

etymology: Perhaps a borrowing from Dutch bunboot, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1671, in a proclamation of Charles II on “Dirt-boats & Bum-boats.” The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) derives it from “boomboats,” because the craft were allowed to tie up to a ship’s boat boom, and mentions an early Low German spelling. The OED marks its own etymology “perhaps.”
biblical_def: A bumboat is a small boat that comes out to ships at anchor to sell provisions, souvenirs and wares to the crew. NHHC says, with some humour, that bumboats were not floating snack bars run by bums or hobos; they were the boats of local traders bringing their goods to the ships, and the name is a hand-me-down from “boomboats,” since they were once allowed to tie up to the boat boom. The OED’s earliest evidence is a 1671 royal proclamation. Bumboat trade has always meant hard bargaining over the rail. The Christian observation: Scripture expects honesty on both sides of the bargain. “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Pro 11:1). Solomon also caught the buyer’s trick: “It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth” (Pro 20:14). And Nehemiah shut the traders out on the sabbath, so that “the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem” (Neh 13:20).
webster_summary: A small boat selling wares and provisions to ships at anchor (OED earliest 1671; perhaps Dutch bunboot); NHHC derives it from “boomboat.” A just weight is the LORD’s delight (Pro 11:1).
webster_full: BUMBOAT, n. (from 1671, OED) A small boat that carries provisions and goods for sale to ships in port or at anchor. Perhaps from Dutch bunboot (OED).
Origin note: NHHC derives it from “boomboat,” from the boat boom the traders tied up to.
scriptures: Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth.
So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice.
corruption_summary: Bumboat trading invites cheating on both sides of the rail; Scripture judges the seller’s false weight and the buyer’s false complaint alike.
corruption_paragraphs: Sailors in a strange port expect to be cheated, and traders expect sailors to haggle. Each side treats deceit as part of the game. Scripture does not. The false balance is an abomination whoever holds it (Pro 11:1).

The buyer who runs down the goods and then boasts of his bargain (Pro 20:14) is no better than the seller who shorts the weight. Honest trade is part of loving one’s neighbour, including the neighbour in a foreign harbour.
roots_summary: Perhaps Dutch bunboot (OED) or boomboat (NHHC) → bumboat (OED earliest 1671) → traders’ boats alongside ships at anchor.
roots_lines: 1671: OED’s earliest evidence, proclamation of Charles II on “Dirt-boats & Bum-boats”
NHHC: from “boomboats,” tied up to the ship’s boat boom; an early Low German spelling
usage: “The bumboats were alongside before the anchor was down.”
A false balance is abomination to the LORD. (Pro 11:1).

etymology: Of unknown origin, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1703, in the writing of the actor and playwright Colley Cibber, and also records a noun from the early 1700s. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) gives it a nautical sense from the days of sail, deceiving another ship by flying a false ensign, but does not claim that the word began at sea.
biblical_def: To bamboozle is to deceive or trick someone, today often as a joke. NHHC records that the word was used in the days of sail without any hilarity: to bamboozle was to deceive a passing vessel about your ship’s origin or nationality by flying an ensign other than your own, a common practice of pirates. The OED calls the word’s origin unknown, and its earliest evidence comes from the theatre, not the sea. The Christian observation: the false flag and the “only joking” deceiver are close cousins. Solomon wrote, “As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?” (Pro 26:18–19). And the greatest of all false colours is the devil’s: “for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2Co 11:14).
webster_summary: To deceive or hoax (OED earliest 1703, origin unknown); at sea, to fly false colours to deceive another ship (NHHC). The deceiver who says “Am not I in sport?” (Pro 26:19).
webster_full: BAMBOOZLE, v.t. (from 1703, OED) To deceive, trick or mystify. Origin unknown (OED).
Nautical note: in the days of sail, to deceive another vessel about one’s nationality by flying a false ensign (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death,
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
corruption_summary: Bamboozle has softened from false colours to a harmless prank; Scripture says the deceiver who pleads “only sport” is a madman throwing firebrands.
corruption_paragraphs: Words for deceit tend to soften with use. A pirate’s false flag became a schoolboy’s prank, and the word now sounds almost friendly. The softening is itself a kind of bamboozling: it teaches us that deception is a game.

Solomon refused the excuse two thousand years before the word existed (Pro 26:18–19). Trust is the ship every community sails in, and a lie told for fun still holes it. The Christian flies his true colours, because his Master is the truth.
roots_summary: Origin unknown (OED; earliest 1703, Colley Cibber) → bamboozle, to deceive → nautical use, false colours (NHHC) → modern sense, a playful trick.
roots_lines: 1703: OED’s earliest evidence, Colley Cibber; also a noun from the early 1700s
Days of sail: deceiving a passing vessel with a false ensign, a pirates’ practice (NHHC)
usage: “The salesman bamboozled him into the extended warranty.”
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport? (Pro 26:19).

etymology: A compound of crow and nest, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1604, in a translation by Edward Grimeston, with the earliest subject listed as military, then whaling and nautical from the 1810s. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains the name from crows carried aboard to find land, whose cages were kept at the masthead; the OED’s earlier military use is not explained by that story.
biblical_def: The crow’s nest is the lookout’s station high on a ship’s mast. NHHC’s account is that crows were part of early navigation: when weather hid the shore, a crow was released, and because it invariably headed for land the navigator steered after it; the cages were kept high on the mainmast where the lookout stood his watch, so he shared his perch with a crow or two. The OED shows the phrase in a military sense in 1604 and in nautical use from the 1810s, so the bird-cage explanation is not settled. The Christian observation: the oldest ship in Scripture used birds the same way. Noah “sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth” (Gen 8:7). And the lookout’s post is the prophet’s: “I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower” (Hab 2:1). God says to Ezekiel, “I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel” (Eze 33:7).
webster_summary: The lookout’s platform high on a mast (OED earliest 1604, crow + nest); NHHC explains it from caged crows released to find land. The watchman upon the tower (Hab 2:1).
webster_full: CROW’S NEST, n. (from 1604, OED) A lookout station at or near the top of a ship’s mast. Compound of crow and nest; OED subjects military (early 1600s), whaling and nautical (1810s).
Origin note: NHHC derives the name from crows carried to find land, caged at the masthead.
scriptures: Gen 8:7
And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.
Hab 2:1
I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.
Eze 33:7
So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me.
corruption_summary: The lookout in the crow’s nest is useless if he will not call what he sees; the pulpit that sees danger and stays silent has abandoned the post.
corruption_paragraphs: A lookout is posted high so that he sees first and calls out first. A lookout who keeps quiet to avoid alarming the passengers has turned his post into a perch. God told Ezekiel that the watchman who sees the sword coming and does not warn the people will answer for their blood (Eze 33:6).

Churches face the same temptation. It is easier to keep watch in silence than to cry out against sin and false teaching. Habakkuk climbed his tower to hear God and then to speak (Hab 2:1); the watchman’s duty is both.
roots_summary: crow + nest (OED earliest 1604, military) → masthead lookout (nautical from the 1810s) → NHHC’s account: caged crows released to find land.
roots_lines: 1604: OED’s earliest evidence, Edward Grimeston; OED subjects military (early 1600s), whaling and nautical (1810s)
NHHC: crows carried to find land in poor visibility; cages at the masthead
usage: “The lookout in the crow’s nest sang out, ‘Land ho!’”
I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower. (Hab 2:1).

etymology: Shanty is probably a borrowing from French chantez, “sing!”, from chanter, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1856, in the writing of C. Nordhoff. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) gives the French chanter explanation and a second one, that the name refers to the shanties on the Mobile, Alabama, waterfront where sailors learned many of the tunes.
biblical_def: A sea shanty is a work song sung by a ship’s crew in the days of sail while heaving on lines or turning the capstan. NHHC explains that the rhythm made every man push or pull at the same moment, so the work went better. It describes three kinds: short-drag shanties for a few strong pulls, long-drag shanties for long hauls, and heaving shanties for steady work such as turning the capstan. A chanty-man stood above the crew and sang the main lines, the men answered on the second, and on the last word they pulled together; a good chanty-man was prized and often excused from other duties to make new verses. The Christian observation: the sea itself sings of God’s works. “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:23–24). Song bound the crew together at their work, and Paul tells the church to teach and admonish “one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). Paul and Silas sang in the stocks at midnight (Act 16:25).
webster_summary: A sailors’ work song that kept a crew pulling together at lines and capstan (NHHC); shanty probably from French chantez (OED earliest 1856). Psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Col 3:16).
webster_full: SHANTY (also chantey, chanty), n. (from 1856, OED) A song sung by sailors at work, to keep time in hauling or heaving. Probably from French chantez (OED).
Kinds: short-drag, long-drag and heaving shanties, led by a chanty-man (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;
These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
corruption_summary: The shanty was sung by the whole crew at the work; the loss is a church that listens to a few performers instead of singing together.
corruption_paragraphs: A shanty only worked if every man sang and pulled. The chanty-man led, but the crew answered, and the line came home on their combined voice. Singing was not entertainment; it was how the work got done together.

Congregational singing was meant to work the same way: the whole church teaching and admonishing one another (Col 3:16). When worship becomes a stage and a silent audience, the church has kept the chanty-man and lost the crew.
roots_summary: French chantez / chanter, to sing (OED: probably; NHHC: some believe) → shanty (OED earliest 1856) → sailors’ work song. NHHC alternative: Mobile waterfront shanties.
roots_lines: 1856: OED’s earliest evidence for shanty in this sense, C. Nordhoff
Short-drag, long-drag and heaving shanties; the chanty-man leads (NHHC)
usage: “The crew sang a heaving shanty as they walked the capstan round.”
They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters. (Psa 107:23).

etymology: From the seams of a wooden ship’s deck. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that the seams between deck planks, packed with oakum and sealed with pitch and tar, made parallel lines along the deck, and that sailors falling in at quarters were directed to stand with their toes just touching a seam; boys and student officers were also made to stand on a seam as a punishment.
biblical_def: To toe the line is to conform to a rule or standard. NHHC traces it to the deck of a wooden warship. The gaps between planks were filled with oakum and sealed with pitch and tar, and from a distance the seams made parallel lines about half a foot apart down the deck. Once a week, usually Sunday, the crew fell in at quarters, and to keep each row straight the men stood with their toes touching a particular seam. The seams were also used for punishment: a ship’s boy or student officer who talked or fidgeted at the wrong time might be made to stand with his toes on a seam, silent, for hours. NHHC concludes that this is where we get our warning to unruly youngsters to “toe the line.” The Christian observation: order in a company of men is a good thing, and Scripture commends it. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Paul rejoiced to behold the Colossians’ “order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ” (Col 2:5). And each man must look to his own feet: “Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established” (Pro 4:26).
webster_summary: To conform to a rule or standard; from sailors standing with their toes on a deck seam at quarters, or as a punishment (NHHC). Decently and in order (1Co 14:40).
webster_full: TOE THE LINE, phr. To conform to a rule, standard or order. From the practice of standing with the toes touching a deck seam when falling in at quarters, and as a punishment for boys and student officers (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Col 2:5
For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.
Pro 4:26
Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Toeing a lawful line is good order; the question is always who drew the line, because no man may be required to toe a line drawn against God’s word.
corruption_paragraphs: The deck seam was a fair standard: straight, fixed and the same for every man. Most lines a Christian is asked to toe are like that, and he should toe them without grumbling. Order is a gift, and Paul rejoiced in it (Col 2:5).

But some lines are drawn by men to bring conscience into line with error. Then the apostles’ answer stands: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The obedient man toes God’s line first, and every other line only as far as it agrees.
roots_summary: Deck seams packed with oakum and pitch → men at quarters with their toes on a seam; boys on a seam as punishment → toe the line, conform (NHHC).
roots_lines: Oakum and pitch-sealed seams about half a foot apart (NHHC)
Weekly quarters, usually Sunday: toes on a seam to align each row (NHHC)
Punishment: standing silent on a seam for hours (NHHC)
usage: “The new hands learned to toe the line in the first week.”
Let all things be done decently and in order. (1Co 14:40).

etymology: Nautical. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) says the statement was first printed on a seaman’s discharge to show that he knew the names and main uses of the principal ropes aboard ship; in other words, that he was a novice who knew only the basics. Its meaning has since shifted to “experienced.”
biblical_def: To know the ropes today means to know one’s way around: to be experienced and capable. NHHC notes that the phrase started with almost the opposite meaning. Printed on a seaman’s discharge, “knows the ropes” meant only that he knew the names and primary uses of the main ropes on board, that is, that he was a novice with the basics of seamanship. The words did not change; the standard behind them did. The Christian observation: Scripture distinguishes clearly between knowing the first principles and being mature. The Hebrews were rebuked because, when they ought to have been teachers, they needed to be taught again “the first principles of the oracles of God” (Heb 5:12). “But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil” (Heb 5:14). The way from one to the other is the way of the learner: “A wise man will hear, and will increase learning” (Pro 1:5).
webster_summary: To be experienced and capable; originally a seaman’s discharge note meaning he knew only the basic ropes, a novice (NHHC). First principles versus full age (Heb 5:12–14).
webster_full: KNOW THE ROPES, phr. To be familiar with how something is done; to be experienced. Originally, a note on a seaman’s discharge that he knew the names and uses of the main ropes, marking a novice (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Heb 5:12

For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Pro 1:5
A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels:
corruption_summary: “Knows the ropes” was promoted from novice to veteran without any more learning; Christians do the same when they mistake knowing the basics for maturity.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase’s drift is a parable. A note that once marked a beginner now marks an old hand, though nothing was added to it. Many believers know the names of the doctrines and assume that makes them mature.

Hebrews says maturity comes by use: senses exercised to discern good and evil (Heb 5:14). Knowing the ropes in the old sense is where every Christian starts, and it is good. Staying there and calling it seamanship is the error.
roots_summary: Seaman’s discharge: “knows the ropes,” the main ropes and their uses (a novice) → know the ropes, experienced (NHHC).
roots_lines: Original sense: printed on a seaman’s discharge, knows the names and primary uses of the main ropes (NHHC)
Modern sense: knows his way around; capable (NHHC)
usage: “Put him with the bosun; he knows the ropes.”
A wise man will hear, and will increase learning. (Pro 1:5).

etymology: Named for the place of the ceremony. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that in the days of sail the captain held it under the mainmast, on a regular basis and usually on a Sunday morning just before divine services, so it came to be called “mast.”
biblical_def: Captain’s mast, or simply mast, is the hearing at which a ship’s commanding officer awards non-judicial punishment for breaches of regulations, or official recognition for jobs well done. NHHC says the ceremony took its name from its location: in the days of sail it was held under the mainmast, regularly, and usually on a Sunday morning just before divine services. The same proceeding both punishes and commends. The Christian observation: that is exactly how Scripture describes lawful authority. Rulers are sent “for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well” (1Pe 2:14). “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil… do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same” (Rom 13:3). And the last mast every man will stand is before the Lord Himself, whose commendation is the one that matters: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21).
webster_summary: The commanding officer’s hearing for non-judicial punishment or commendation, named for being held under the mainmast, usually Sunday before divine services (NHHC). Authority punishes evil and praises good (1Pe 2:14).
webster_full: CAPTAIN’S MAST (also mast), n. (Navy) A proceeding at which the commanding officer awards non-judicial punishment for offenses, or recognition for good work. From its being held under the mainmast (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.
Rom 13:3
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: Mast was built to punish and to praise; authority that only punishes breeds fear, and authority that only praises breeds contempt.
corruption_paragraphs: A ship where mast means only punishment teaches its crew to hide. A ship where nothing is ever punished teaches its crew that the rules are a joke. NHHC’s description of mast holds both together, and so does Peter: punishment of evildoers and praise of them that do well (1Pe 2:14).

Fathers, pastors and officers fall into one error or the other. The old practice of holding mast just before divine service is a good reminder that every captain answers to a higher Captain, who will one day both judge and commend (Mat 25:21).
roots_summary: mast (the mainmast) → ceremony held under it, usually Sunday before divine services → captain’s mast, non-judicial punishment or recognition (NHHC).
roots_lines: Days of sail: held under the mainmast, usually Sunday morning before divine services (NHHC)
Modern Navy: non-judicial punishment or official recognition by the commanding officer
usage: “He went to captain’s mast for missing ship’s movement.”
Do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same. (Rom 13:3).

etymology: From tending the side. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that in the days of sail, visitors, including officers coming to conferences or dinner on another ship, were often hoisted aboard in a boatswain’s chair, and the crewmen who did the hoisting at the side were the sideboys. NHHC calls it a custom inherited from the British Navy.
biblical_def: Sideboys are the sailors, in clean uniforms, who line up on the quarterdeck when visiting dignitaries come aboard. NHHC traces the custom to the days of sail, when gangways were seldom used and men boarded by climbing rope ladders. Important visitors were often hoisted aboard in a boatswain’s chair rigged from a yardarm, and the crew who did the heaving tended the side; that is where the honour came from. NHHC adds, half in jest, that some have reported the higher the rank, the heavier the man, and so the more sideboys. The Christian observation: Scripture commands honour where honour is due. “Render therefore to all their dues… fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour” (Rom 13:7). “Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17). And among brothers the rule runs both ways: “in honour preferring one another” (Rom 12:10).
webster_summary: Sailors lined up on the quarterdeck to honour visiting dignitaries; from the men who hoisted visitors aboard in a boatswain’s chair (NHHC). Honour to whom honour (Rom 13:7).
webster_full: SIDEBOYS (also side boys), n. pl. (Navy) Sailors in clean uniforms lined up on the quarterdeck to honour visiting dignitaries coming aboard. From the crewmen who tended the side and hoisted visitors aboard (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Rom 13:7
Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
corruption_summary: The sideboys’ honour began as hard service to a visitor; ceremony that keeps the honour and forgets the service has lost its meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: The first sideboys did real work: they hauled a man aboard who could not climb. The ceremony that grew from it is a fitting honour, but its root is a reminder that honour in a Christian sense is shown by serving.

Our age tends to despise ceremony as empty or to keep it only for show. Scripture asks for honour to whom honour is due (Rom 13:7), given by men who would also lift the load, because they prefer one another in honour (Rom 12:10).
roots_summary: Days of sail: visitors hoisted aboard in a boatswain’s chair → crewmen tending the side → sideboys, a rank of honour at the gangway (NHHC).
roots_lines: Conferences and dinners at sea; visitors hoisted aboard from a yardarm (NHHC)
Custom inherited from the British Navy (NHHC)
usage: “Eight sideboys and the bosun’s pipe for the admiral.”
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king. (1Pe 2:17).

etymology: An order and method of freeing a grounded ship. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that the crew gathered along one side and ran together from port to starboard and back until the ship began to roll, which could break the suction of the mud.
biblical_def: To sally ship was to rock a grounded vessel free. NHHC notes that “sally ship” was not a ship at all but a method: before modern navigation, ships ran aground far more often, and a ship stuck in mud could often be freed with little or no damage if she could be rocked loose. The order was given, the whole crew lined up along one side, and on command they ran athwartships from port to starboard and back again until the ship began to roll. The rolling often broke the mud’s grip, and she could be pulled free and got under way. It worked only if every man ran together. The Christian observation: Paul’s ship ran aground too, “and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable” (Act 27:41). Scripture’s answer to being stuck is often the same as the Navy’s: many hands together. “Two are better than one… For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecc 4:9–10). “Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2).
webster_summary: To free a grounded ship by having the whole crew run from side to side together until she rolls loose (NHHC). Bear one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2).
webster_full: SALLY SHIP, n. and v. phr. (Navy) The method, and the order, of rocking a grounded ship free by having the crew run together from one side to the other (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: No sailor can sally a ship alone; the error is the individualism that leaves a brother stuck fast because no one will run with him.
corruption_paragraphs: A grounded ship does not respond to one strong man. It responds to the whole crew moving together, in time, on command. Modern Christianity often treats a stuck brother as his own problem: let him pray harder and find his own way off the mud.

Solomon said the opposite: woe to him that is alone when he falls (Ecc 4:10). The law of Christ is fulfilled by bearing one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2). The church sallies ship when the whole congregation moves for one member.
roots_summary: “sally ship,” the order to run the crew side to side → grounded ship rolled free (NHHC).
roots_lines: Before modern navigation, groundings were frequent (NHHC)
Method: crew in a line along one side, running athwartships until the ship rolls (NHHC)
usage: “The captain ordered all hands to sally ship, and she came off the bar on the third roll.”
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. (Gal 6:2).

etymology: Nautical. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that strict officers in the old Navy did not let sailors gather and tell stories, except on the one weekly job that required them to sit together: unravelling the strands of old line.
