That period became the time for “spinning yarns,” and later anyone telling a tale was said to be spinning a yarn.
biblical_def: To spin a yarn is to tell a long story, usually an exaggerated or tall one. NHHC says that it was first a sailors’ term. Officers and mates in the old Navy were stern disciplinarians who believed that if men were allowed to gather and tell sea stories, no work would be done. But one job required congregating once a week: unravelling the strands of old line to make yarn for other uses. On that day the men could talk to their hearts’ content, and the period came to be known as the time for “spinning yarns.” The Christian observation: Scripture does not forbid a good story, and our Lord taught in parables. But it does weigh our words. “In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise” (Pro 10:19). “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6). And every word, the yarns included, will be accounted for: “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment” (Mat 12:36).
webster_summary: To tell a long, often exaggerated story; from sailors talking while unravelling old line into yarn (NHHC). Speech seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).
webster_full: SPIN A YARN, phr. To tell a long or tall story. From the weekly shipboard task of unravelling old line, when sailors were allowed to talk (Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
corruption_summary: A sea story is good fellowship; a yarn becomes sin when the exaggeration turns into a lie that someone is meant to believe.
corruption_paragraphs: Sailors have always known the difference between a yarn and a report. Everyone at the table knows the yarn is stretched, and the stretching is part of the fun. That is not deceit, because no one is deceived.

The line is crossed when the tale is meant to be believed, when it makes the teller a hero at another man’s expense, or when it fills the hours that should go to work. Words are weighed (Mat 12:36), and the wise man knows when to stop talking (Pro 10:19).
roots_summary: Weekly unravelling of old line into yarn → the one time sailors could talk at length → spinning a yarn, telling a tale (NHHC).
roots_lines: Old Navy: officers discouraged sailors from gathering to tell stories (NHHC)
Weekly exception: unravelling the strands of old line (NHHC)
Later: any long or tall tale
usage: “Grandpa was spinning a yarn about a typhoon off Okinawa.”
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt. (Col 4:6).

etymology: Nautical. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that in the days of sail, when a good breeze came, the officer of the deck ordered the crew to “carry on,” meaning to hoist every bit of canvas the yards could carry. Today the Bluejacket’s Manual defines it as an order to resume work.
biblical_def: Carry on is the Navy’s order to resume what one was doing. NHHC says that it began as a sailing order. The officer of the deck watched constantly for any change in the wind so that sail could be reefed or added to make the best speed. Whenever a good breeze came, he gave the order to “carry on”: to set every sail the yards could carry. A ship caught partly reefed when a good breeze arrived lost her chance, and the sailor whose weather eye failed him paid for it. Over the centuries the meaning shifted to the modern order to resume work. The Christian observation: the old sense is the believer’s calling, to use every opportunity God sends. “He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap” (Ecc 11:4). “And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9). Paul set every sail he had: “I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Php 3:14).
webster_summary: The order to resume work; originally, under sail, to set every sail the yards could carry when a good breeze came (NHHC). Be not weary in well doing (Gal 6:9).
webster_full: CARRY ON, v. phr. (Navy) 1. Originally, to set all the sail the yards can carry in a good breeze. 2. An order to resume work or one’s previous activity (Bluejacket’s Manual, per the Naval History and Heritage Command).
scriptures: Ecc 11:4
He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Php 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: “Carry on” once meant crowding on sail when the wind came; the drift to “keep doing what you were doing” can hide the loss of zeal it first commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: The original order was an order to seize the moment: the breeze has come, so set everything. The modern order often means little more than “as you were.” Both are useful, but the first is the one the Christian life needs.

Solomon warned the man who waits for perfect weather (Ecc 11:4). The opposite failure is to be caught reefed when God sends the wind. The believer carries on in the old sense: not weary in well doing (Gal 6:9), pressing toward the mark (Php 3:14).
roots_summary: Days of sail: “carry on,” set all sail in a good breeze → modern Navy order to resume work (NHHC; Bluejacket’s Manual).
roots_lines: Officer of the deck watching the wind to reef or add sail (NHHC)
Modern sense: an order to resume work (Bluejacket’s Manual, per NHHC)
usage: “The captain returned the salute and said, ‘Carry on.’”
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. (Gal 6:9).
